questions.question_stem: You trace a 3.00 BTC ransom forward. The ransom address spends it in one transaction with two outputs: 1.00 BTC to an address used many times before, and 1.9993 BTC to a never-used address of the same script type. (a) Write this hop as your trace notes must record it. (b) How sure can the hop be, and what would raise it? (c) Two hops later the trail goes cold, but you know a service deposit address where the suspect later cashed out. What can you do, and what must you note?
answer_key: Where the money went: the 1.9993 BTC output is the likely change, so the trace follows it; the 1.00 BTC payment is recorded as a lead.
The heuristic: change detection, from a fresh address, the same script type and an un-round amount.
What could make it wrong: change is a guess from weak clues (a payee can use a fresh address too).
How sure: Moderate, because several clues agree (one alone is Low); same-transaction clues never reach High alone, so another kind of evidence would raise it.
Trace backward from that deposit, where the money ended, and record the direction: backward tracing gives more false positives.
questions.explanation: Every hop names where the money went, the heuristic, what could make it wrong and how sure. Several change clues agreeing are Moderate; clues from one transaction never reach High without another kind of evidence. Backward tracing works when forward fails, but gives more false positives.

concept.name: Clustering heuristics and tracing patterns (e.g. peel chains)

questions.question_stem: (a) Transaction A spends coins from addresses X and Y together as its inputs. What does that suggest about X and Y, and how sure? (b) Transaction B has 50 inputs and 50 outputs of exactly the same amount. Do you link its inputs to one owner? Why? (c) Further on, a 400 BTC coin passes through 25 transactions; each sends a small amount to a new address and the rest on to the next. Name the pattern, say which side you follow, and say what you record for each small payment.
answer_key: A: co-spending suggests X and Y have one owner; Moderate on its own.
B: it looks like a CoinJoin, many owners in one transaction, so its inputs are not linked; one false link would merge different actors into one cluster.
C: a peel chain; follow the remainder (the large output) hop by hop, treating each peel as a lead.
For each peel record the amount, the address, the hop number and the next action; the first peel that lands at a service ends the trace.
questions.explanation: Co-spending is the base of Bitcoin clustering, but only Moderate alone, and a CoinJoin breaks it: one false link merges two actors into one. A peel chain sends small peels off while the remainder rolls on; follow the remainder and log each peel as a lead.

Follow the remainder; the peels are your leads

questions.question_stem: A clinic received a ransom note and paid. The agent on the case asks you to trace the payment. (a) What do you ask the victim for? (b) Where did the clinic most likely get the coin? (c) Your trace reaches a wallet that holds most of the ransom and has not moved. How do you state where the trace ended?
answer_key: Ask for the ransom address and the payment transaction, the note and its Tor address, the chat on the payment portal, and who bought the coins and where.
The clinic, or a DFIR firm paying for it, most likely bought the coin at an exchange.
Say the trace stopped at a wallet, not at a service, and give the date the balance was checked.
questions.explanation: The note, the portal and the chat are leads the victim holds; the ransom address and payment transaction start the trace. The victim usually buys the coin at an exchange, sometimes through a DFIR firm. A trace that stops at an unmoved wallet says so, with the date the balance was checked.

questions.question_stem: A $6M ransom reaches the ransomware group's address. Its first hop splits it about 10% and 90% to two new wallets. If the group runs ransomware as a service, what does the split most likely show, and how sure can you be from the amounts alone?
questions.correct_answer: The developer's cut and the affiliate's share; Low from the amounts alone.
incorrect_answers: Payment and change from one owner; High, since the larger share is round.
Two separate gangs sharing one victim; Moderate, as both wallets are new.
The exchange fee and the ransom; High, since exchanges skim each payout.
questions.explanation: In RaaS the developer rents the ransomware to affiliates and takes a cut on chain; DarkSide's cut fell from 25% to 10% as ransoms grew. A share read from the amounts alone is Low.

questions.question_stem: Hydra was the largest darknet market when it was sanctioned in April 2022. Why does a market like Hydra matter to a trace of ransomware proceeds?
questions.correct_answer: It is both a shop, selling RaaS and other services, and a place to cash out.
incorrect_answers: It is a mixer only, pooling coins so no trace can pass through to a buyer.
It takes only Monero, so a payment into it ends any Bitcoin trace for good.
It is a licensed exchange whose KYC records name every buyer and seller.
questions.explanation: A darknet market is both a shop (Hydra sold RaaS and other services) and a cash-out: about $8M of ransom went through Hydra, and most illicit BTC that Russian exchanges received directly in 2019 came from it.

questions.question_stem: A forum post under an alias lists a Bitcoin address, and the alias was used from IP addresses near the suspect's home. How should the analyst weigh this open-source information?
questions.correct_answer: As a lead that needs another line of evidence before it supports a finding.
incorrect_answers: As proof of ownership, since the suspect posted the address in public online.
As High confidence, since two pieces of open-source data agree on one address.
As worthless, since anything posted online is too easily faked to be any use.
questions.explanation: OSINT such as an alias, forum posts or IP addresses is a lead that needs another line of evidence. Two OSINT items are still one kind; confidence counts kinds of evidence.

questions.question_stem: An address in your trace carries the tag "Mixer M" on one commercial platform, with no stated basis. (a) What confidence does that attribution carry? (b) A second platform's clustering also puts it in a Mixer M cluster: what now? (c) Then a government release lists that exact address as Mixer M's, and your own test deposits land in the platform's cluster for M: what now? (d) What three questions do you ask of every label?
answer_key: One tag with an unknown basis: Low.
Two platforms' clusters agree: Moderate, because they are one kind of evidence.
A government label for the exact address, plus the cluster your test deposits confirm: High, a cluster plus a label of another kind.
Ask of every label: who says so, how they knew, and how it could be wrong.
questions.explanation: Attribution confidence counts kinds of evidence. One tag of unknown basis is Low; two platforms' clusters agreeing are still one kind, Moderate; a cluster plus a label of another kind is High. Every label answers who says so, how they knew and how it could be wrong.

concept.name: Commercial analytics platforms, as a category

questions.question_stem: A commercial analytics platform puts a suspect's address in a cluster of over 200 million addresses and reports that its clustering is 99.9% accurate. What is the right reading?
questions.correct_answer: It runs your heuristics at scale; 99.9% describes its method, not your link.
incorrect_answers: It has checked more data than any analyst, so the cluster is High as given.
Its method is secret, so courts refuse every trace built with its clusters.
Its labels are read from the chain, so they need no other source at all.
questions.explanation: Platforms run the same heuristics (co-spend, change, intelligence labels) at scale. A huge cluster with no label is Low, and a platform's accuracy figure describes its method, not your link.

concept.name: Explaining findings to agents, prosecutors and leadership

questions.question_stem: You traced a victim's 5 BTC through three hops, each following likely change (Moderate), to a deposit address that the exchange's records show belongs to one customer account. The agent, who is not a specialist, asks what you found. Write your explanation in the course's five parts.
answer_key: Bottom line first: the victim's bitcoin most likely reached an account at the exchange.
What the evidence shows: the transactions, amounts and addresses, hop by hop, to the deposit address, which the exchange's record ties to one account.
What is inferred: that each change output stayed with the same holder (the change heuristic).
How confident, in a course word with its reason, never a percentage: each change hop is Moderate on its own.
What it cannot show: who controls the account or who stole the coins; that needs the exchange's records and other evidence off chain.
questions.explanation: The five parts: bottom line first, what the chain shows, what is inferred, how confident (a course word), and what the evidence cannot show. Who did it comes from records off chain.

questions.question_stem: (a) A transaction has 5 inputs and 5 outputs of exactly 0.05 BTC each. What is it likely to be, and what does that mean for your clustering? (b) Later, one of those outputs is spent together with a coin from the suspect's known address. What does that show, and how sure? (c) Elsewhere, the suspect sends 2 BTC into a custodial mixer. How do you treat the coins that come out? (d) If only timing links a deposit to a withdrawal, how sure is the link?
answer_key: A CoinJoin (equal outputs, like a Whirlpool 5x5 in the 0.05 pool): many owners in one transaction, so mark it and don't cluster across it.
The post-mix co-spend with the suspect's coin links that output to the suspect: Moderate.
A custodial mixer pools coins and pays out others: label the mixer and treat each withdrawal as a new start.
Timing alone is Low.
questions.explanation: Equal outputs mark a CoinJoin; mark it and don't cluster across it. Before and after the mix still leak: a post-mix co-spend is Moderate, timing alone Low. A custodial mixer pays out other coins, so each withdrawal is a new start.

questions.question_stem: A Monero transaction from 2025 spends one input with a ring of 16. The agent asks which ring member was really spent. What do you answer?
questions.correct_answer: Undetermined: the ring hides the real spend among 15 decoys.
incorrect_answers: The newest member: it is the real spend in most Monero rings.
The one whose address the explorer shows beside the input field.
The largest one: RingCT shows each ring member's amount in clear.
questions.explanation: A ring hides the real spend among 15 decoys; which member was spent is Undetermined. Newest-is-real worked on old Monero, before the fixes, so date the transaction.

questions.question_stem: Malware mining Monero on a company's cloud servers ran up a $210,000 bill. The mining pool shows the criminal's wallet earned about $4,000. What loss do you report?
questions.correct_answer: The $210,000 cloud bill; never the miner's earnings.
incorrect_answers: The $4,000 mined, the only value that moved on chain.
Nothing: no coins left any wallet the firm owns.
$214,000: the bill plus the coins the miner took.
questions.explanation: Cryptojacking steals computing power, not coins: the proceeds start as new coin, and in the cloud the victim pays the bill. Report the bill as the loss, never the miner's earnings.

questions.question_stem: NFT #412 sold from wallet A to B, B to C, and C back to A, each a paid sale on a marketplace. B and C were funded by the address that funded A. How sure can you be that these were wash trades?
questions.correct_answer: Moderate: paid sales, self-financed by the seller's side; repeated, with a payoff: High.
incorrect_answers: High: a token that comes back to its first owner is wash trading by its very own definition.
Low: friends trading fit the loop, so the shared funding adds nothing to the case.
Undetermined: marketplaces hide each buyer, so funding cannot be traced back at all.
questions.explanation: A loop alone is Low; paid sales with buyers self-financed by the seller's side are Moderate, because one party sits on both sides. Repetition with a payoff (a later buyer, a ranking, reward tokens) makes it High.

questions.question_stem: A DeFi lending pool loses $40M in one transaction, and no one's private key was stolen. What makes this possible?
questions.correct_answer: The pool is a contract anyone may call; a gap in its rules lets a caller drain it.
incorrect_answers: Every depositor shares the pool's admin key, so any of them can sign the withdrawals.
The pool lends to every wallet that asks, with no collateral and no repayment ever due.
The pool's code is hidden, so a caller can change it after the users have deposited.
questions.explanation: A DeFi protocol keeps deposits in a contract that anyone, including another contract, may call. When its rules have a gap, the caller takes the pool, with no key needed. Find the protocol and its write-up first.

questions.question_stem: One transaction starts with 20M USDC in from Aave and ends with 20,010,000 USDC back to Aave. In between are trades on two exchanges. No pool or protocol shows a loss. What can you say?
questions.correct_answer: A flash loan was used (High); with no loss or write-up, it may be arbitrage.
incorrect_answers: An attack (High): flash loans exist only to supply attackers with their capital.
A default: Aave lost the 20M, and the extra 10,000 is a late-payment fine.
A theft from Aave: lenders bear the risk the loan will not come back.
questions.explanation: A flash loan shows in the transfers, so its use is High. A flash loan alone is not an attack: without a victim's loss or a write-up the transaction may be arbitrage.

questions.question_stem: A call trace shows withdraw, pay, withdraw, pay, nested inside each other, all paying one contract, and the pool lost far more than that contract deposited. What is it, and how sure can you be from the trace alone?
questions.correct_answer: Reentrancy: Moderate from the trace alone, High with the write-up.
incorrect_answers: A flash loan: High, since all of the money returned in one go.
Reentrancy: High alone, as nested calls are never legitimate.
A moved oracle: Moderate, since the pool paid at a wrong price.
questions.explanation: Nested repeat calls paying one contract, with a loss larger than the deposit, read as reentrancy: Moderate from the trace alone, High with the protocol's write-up. Without the loss, Low: some contracts call back legitimately.

questions.question_stem: A lending pool values collateral at the spot price of one thin exchange pool. What is the attack risk, and which defense fits it?
questions.correct_answer: A big borrowed trade moves the price it reads; a TWAP or an oracle network resists it.
incorrect_answers: Its code can be re-entered while it is paying out; recording balances first stops it.
Users may sign approvals on phishing sites; revoking them all to zero stops that risk.
Its admin key may be stolen; requiring five of nine validator keys to sign stops it all.
questions.explanation: A large trade, paid for with a flash loan, moves the spot price the lender reads, so it lends too much against the collateral (bZx, 2020). A time-weighted average price or a decentralized oracle network resists a recent large trade.

questions.question_stem: A contract has no verified source. You decompile its bytecode, and a signature database names one function's selector, 0xa9059cbb, as transfer(address,uint256). How sure can you be about what that function does?
questions.correct_answer: Moderate at best from the decompiled code; the name is only a lead.
incorrect_answers: High: a selector is a hash of the signature, so it proves the action.
High: decompiling restores the source's names, comments and intent.
None: without verified source no confidence word applies at all.
questions.explanation: A selector lookup gives the name someone registered, not proof of behavior. A decompiler recovers structure, not names or intent, and can be wrong: decompiled code alone is Moderate at best; logs that agree raise it.

questions.question_stem: A victim's USDC left in a transaction sent by another address, yet the victim's own history shows no approve. What should you look for?
questions.correct_answer: A permit: an Approval event inside the spender's own transaction.
incorrect_answers: A stolen key: only the owner's key moves tokens without an approve.
A poisoning: a zero-value lure from a look-alike moved the tokens.
A clipboard hijacker: the victim pasted the thief's spender address.
questions.explanation: A permit sets an allowance from a message signed off chain: the spender puts the signature on chain, so the Approval event sits inside the spender's transaction and the victim's history shows no approve.

questions.question_stem: A victim sent 2 ETH from their own address to an unknown address. There is no look-alike lure and no approval, and the address resembles no past payee. What can you say from the chain?
questions.correct_answer: Wrong recipient, cause not on chain; a clipper is possible but Low, with proof on the device.
incorrect_answers: Address poisoning, High: a wrong recipient is exactly how every poisoning ends up on the chain.
A drainer, Moderate: the thief moved the ETH under an approval the victim gave earlier.
A stolen key, High: the owner's address sent it, so the thief must hold the private key.
questions.explanation: Without a lure, the chain shows only a wrong recipient. A clipboard hijacker is possible, but the proof is on the device, so on chain evidence alone it is Low.

questions.question_stem: In March 2022 the Ronin bridge lost about $620M through withdrawals signed with stolen validator keys. What does the chain show about this theft, and where does the name "North Korea" come from?
questions.correct_answer: Where the funds went, through mixers and to Bitcoin; the name is the FBI's, quoted with its date.
incorrect_answers: Who took them, since validator keys tied to Lazarus signed each one of the bridge withdrawals directly.
Nothing at all, since mixers hid every movement and the government's name is only a guess.
Where the funds went; the analyst names North Korea from the laundering pattern on its own.
questions.explanation: The chain shows where the funds went: through a mixer on Ethereum, then to Bitcoin and a Bitcoin mixer. The FBI named Lazarus Group on 14 April 2022; the analyst quotes that attribution as the FBI's, with its date.

concept.name: MITRE ATT&CK and the Diamond Model

questions.question_stem: You place a theft on the Diamond Model and find that the thief's infrastructure includes a deposit address at an exchange. What does pivoting from that address along an edge give you?
questions.correct_answer: A lead to check, not a conclusion; each vertex keeps its own confidence.
incorrect_answers: A conclusion about the adversary, as infrastructure is the same vertex.
An ATT&CK technique ID, as each Diamond edge maps to exactly one of them.
High confidence for the whole Diamond, as one confirmed vertex fixes them all.
questions.explanation: The Diamond records four features of one event: adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim, each with its own confidence. A pivot along an edge gives a lead, not a conclusion.

concept.name: Fusing on-chain, OSINT, darknet and classified data

questions.question_stem: Three vendors tag an address "Group X (sanctioned)". All three tags cite the same Treasury release. How many lines of evidence is that, and how sure?
questions.correct_answer: One line, since all three echo one release: Moderate.
incorrect_answers: Three lines, one for each vendor tag: High overall.
Three lines, but each vendor tag alone is Low, so: Low.
None, as vendor tags never count as a source at all.
questions.explanation: Count origins, not labels: three tags copied from one release are one line, Moderate. An echo is not a second line.

questions.question_stem: A blockchain-analytics firm's April report says North Korea "likely" carried out a new theft, citing staging through a mixer and activity in Pyongyang working hours. The US government has said nothing yet. How do you write this in your assessment?
questions.correct_answer: As the firm's assessment, with its name and date: "[Firm] assesses (April) that North Korea likely..."
incorrect_answers: As a government attribution, since the firm's evidence fits the playbook that the state is known to use.
As your own finding at High, since two independent indicators both point to the same state actor.
Not at all: only the government may name a state, so a firm's view is never reported in writing.
questions.explanation: You characterize; the government attributes. A firm's assessment is quoted as the firm's, with its date, never as a government attribution or as your own finding.

questions.question_stem: Funds stolen in a scam leave as USDT, are swapped to ETH on a decentralized exchange, cross a bridge to another chain, reach Bitcoin, go through a CoinJoin, then run down a series of hops that each send a small amount to a new address, ending at an OTC broker. (a) Name the typology at each stage. (b) How do you record the bridge crossing in your trace? (c) Which stages lack an AADAPT entry?
answer_key: The swap out of USDT, away from a token that can be frozen: chain-hopping or the scam cash-out (either is right).
The bridge and the move to Bitcoin: chain-hopping.
The CoinJoin: mixers and CoinJoin; the hops with small payments: a peel chain.
The OTC broker at the end: OTC and nested services, or the scam cash-out's exit (either is right).
Record each chain crossing as its own link, with its own confidence.
AADAPT has no entry for OTC and nested services or for the scam cash-out.
questions.explanation: The course's six typologies: peel chain, CoinJoin and mixers, chain-hopping, OTC and nested services, scam cash-out and drainer flows. A chain crossing is its own link with its own confidence. Moving out of a freezable token can be read as chain-hopping (the Bybit swap) or as the scam cash-out, and an OTC exit as OTC and nested services or as the scam cash-out's end; either label is right. AADAPT names most typologies, but OTC and scam cash-out have no entry.
